guardrails.rule: Never describe a participant's brain, hormones, vagal state or nervous system. Brain and body research is group-level context only.
Never label a statement as a lie or as truthful from its wording, hesitations or style.
Report stage directions such as '[laughs]' or '[sighs]' as annotations; do not infer tone, emotion or intent from them.

Polyvagal states, 'fawn response', 'trauma bond', 'Stockholm syndrome', 'amygdala hijack', 'ego depletion' and 'love hormone' are contested or popular terms. Use plain language in findings and keep the terms for the Knowledge Base.
Suggest a possible DARVO sequence only when deny, attack and reversal all appear in response to a specific concern, and quote each part.
Coercive control is a pattern over time. Say what one transcript can and cannot show, and code only quoted behaviours.
Silence, stillness, going along or absence of resistance is never treated as consent.
Consensual non-monogamy, hierarchy or unusual structure is never itself a red flag; examine agreements, power and freedom to refuse.
Prevalence figures and average effects describe populations, not the people in a transcript.
Different memories of an event are expected; separate each person's report from what can be established.
Items on the watchlist were found but not read; do not cite them for any claim until reviewed.

concepts.title: What brain studies can and cannot tell you
concepts.definition: Brain research describes averages across groups of people in controlled settings. It cannot read the mind of a person in a conversation.
concepts.evidence: Activity in a brain region rarely maps onto one mental process, so 'region X lit up, therefore they felt Y' is weak reasoning. Common brain measures are not reliable enough to assess individuals, small studies inflate effects, and different analysts can reach different conclusions from the same data.
concepts.application: Every brain-related card carries a 'group-level finding' badge. Subtext never describes a participant's brain, hormones or nervous system.
concepts.limitations: Any statement about what was happening in a participant's brain or body during the conversation.
avoidTerms: their brain was in fight mode

concepts.title: Social pain: rejection, exclusion and being ignored
concepts.definition: Being rejected, excluded or ignored is distressing for most people, and research treats it as a real form of pain, not oversensitivity.
concepts.evidence: Early brain studies suggested rejection and physical pain share circuitry; later work found their brain patterns are distinguishable and that exclusion strongly engages regions used to think about oneself and others. Ostracism threatens belonging, self-esteem and control. A 2026 study linked stronger neural sensitivity to peer rejection with lower daily mood in adolescents.
concepts.application: Explains why dismissal, silent treatment or being left out of a decision can matter, without ranking anyone's pain.
concepts.limitations: That a participant intended to exclude someone, or how much it hurt them.
lookFor: A concern or bid that receives no reply or a topic change
Explicit exclusion from a decision or plan
avoidTerms: rejection is literally the same as physical pain

concepts.title: Feeling understood versus dismissed
concepts.definition: Validation means showing you understand what someone said and why it matters to them. It does not mean agreeing.
concepts.evidence: Feeling understood is associated with reward- and connection-related brain activity, while feeling misunderstood is associated with negative affect. In experiments, invalidating replies increased negative emotion and physiological arousal. Being listened to well is associated with less defensiveness. Suppressing emotion during a conversation can raise the other person's stress.
concepts.application: Basis for the acknowledgment / dismissal codes and for 'reflect first' scripts in the Response Playbook.
concepts.limitations: How a specific reply made a participant feel.
lookFor: Restating the other person's point before responding
Replies that dismiss ('you're overreacting') versus acknowledge ('I hear that this hurt')

concepts.title: Thinking under threat
concepts.definition: When people feel threatened or judged, it becomes harder to think flexibly, hold several points in mind and listen.
concepts.evidence: Acute stress impairs working memory and flexible thinking. Being judged by others combined with feeling out of control produces the strongest stress-hormone responses in laboratory studies. Much of the mechanism research is in animals.
concepts.application: Supports pause-and-return scripts and the suggestion to revisit hard topics when everyone is calmer. Applies to all participants equally.
concepts.limitations: That stress excuses conduct, or that a particular person was too stressed to be responsible.
lookFor: Requests to pause or come back later
Escalating speed or repetition in the record (as typed, not inferred tone)

concepts.title: Hostile conflict and health
concepts.definition: Relationship quality and repeated hostile conflict are linked to physical health, though average effects are small.
concepts.evidence: Hostile couples healed experimental wounds more slowly in a small laboratory study; a large meta-analysis found better marital quality associated with better health, with small average effects.
concepts.application: Context for why patterns of hostility matter over time.
concepts.limitations: That a specific relationship is damaging someone's health.

concepts.title: Freezing and tonic immobility
concepts.definition: Under severe threat, some people go still, go quiet or cannot move. This is a recognised defensive response, not a choice to agree.
concepts.evidence: Freezing is an active defensive state. Tonic immobility has been reported by many survivors of sexual assault and predicted later PTSD and depression in one clinical cohort, but prevalence estimates vary widely across studies. Law in several countries does not fully reflect this research.
concepts.application: Grounds the rule that silence, stillness or absence of resistance is never treated as consent.
concepts.limitations: Whether a participant froze during any reported event; whether a reported event occurred.
lookFor: Reports of going quiet, going still or being unable to respond
Others treating that silence as agreement

concepts.title: Fawning and appeasement
concepts.definition: Placating, agreeing or caretaking to stay safe around someone who feels threatening.
concepts.evidence: 'Fawn' comes from clinical writing (Pete Walker) rather than experimental research. Peer-reviewed work has proposed 'appeasement' as a survival strategy and 'tend-and-befriend' as a stress response, but these are theories, and the appeasement paper draws on the contested polyvagal theory.
concepts.application: Use as a possible explanation the user can consider about their own experience, clearly labelled as a clinical formulation.
concepts.limitations: That a participant was fawning; that agreement in a transcript was not genuine.
lookFor: The user describing agreeing or apologising to keep things calm (only as the user's own account)

concepts.title: Polyvagal theory (contested)
concepts.definition: A popular theory that links feelings of safety and danger to specific branches of the vagus nerve.
concepts.evidence: Widely used in therapy and self-help. In 2026, 39 physiologists and neuroscientists concluded its core physiological and evolutionary premises are not supported, including the use of heart-rate variability as a direct measure of vagal 'tone'.
concepts.application: Explain the theory so users recognise the terms, and translate them into plain language ('felt unsafe', 'shut down').
concepts.limitations: Any participant's 'vagal state'; 'ventral', 'dorsal' or 'sympathetic' labels for people in a transcript.

concepts.title: Two-brain research during conversation
concepts.definition: 'Hyperscanning' records two people's brains at once to see how their activity lines up during interaction.
concepts.evidence: Recent studies found synchrony dropped during scripted conflict and was higher between friends sharing negative experiences. The field is young, samples are small and tasks are artificial.
concepts.application: Educational card only.
concepts.limitations: Anything about synchrony, connection or empathy between the people in a transcript.

concepts.title: Oxytocin and trust (popular claim)
concepts.definition: Oxytocin is often called the 'love' or 'trust' hormone.
concepts.evidence: A 2005 study found oxytocin increased trust in an economic game, but replications were weak, and a 2025 systematic review found dose effects on social cognition remain mixed.
concepts.application: Use to correct the popular claim.
concepts.limitations: Any link between a participant's hormones and their trust or attachment.

concepts.title: Emotion regulation strategies
concepts.definition: The ways people influence their own feelings: changing the situation, shifting attention, reframing, or holding back expression.
concepts.evidence: Reframing (reappraisal) has small-to-moderate benefits on average and engages frontal control regions; suppressing expression changes outward behaviour more than inner feeling and can strain the conversation partner.
concepts.application: Language for Response Playbook options; never prescribes how a person should feel.
concepts.limitations: Which strategy a participant used.
lookFor: Stated strategies such as 'I need a minute', 'let me think about it'

concepts.title: Naming feelings (affect labelling)
concepts.definition: Putting a feeling into words, such as 'I feel scared', 'I feel dismissed'.
concepts.evidence: Labelling emotions reduces emotional reactivity in laboratory studies. Nonviolent Communication builds on naming feelings and needs; its evidence base is small and mostly from health-care training.
concepts.application: Supports optional 'I feel / I need' scripts, labelled as practitioner techniques.
concepts.limitations: That naming a feeling obliges anyone to explain or justify it.
lookFor: 'I feel…' statements
Feelings stated without being argued over

concepts.title: Calming each other (interpersonal emotion regulation)
concepts.definition: People often regulate feelings with and through others: seeking comfort, or soothing someone else.
concepts.evidence: Frameworks describe regulating one's own emotions through others and regulating someone else's. A small brain study found a partner's hand-holding reduced threat responses, more so in higher-quality relationships.
concepts.application: Frames requests for reassurance as ordinary. Also supports the rule that nobody must soothe someone before their refusal counts.
concepts.limitations: That any adult is responsible for managing another adult's feelings.
lookFor: Requests for reassurance or comfort
Demands that one person calm another before a refusal is accepted

concepts.title: Apology and repair
concepts.definition: Repair means acknowledging impact and responsibility and changing what happens next.
concepts.evidence: Acknowledging responsibility and offering to repair are the most valued parts of an apology. Insincere apologies had little effect on how observers judged a sexual-assault scenario. Apology is one of several factors associated with forgiveness.
concepts.application: Structures the 'accountable reformulation' scripts and the repair codes.
concepts.limitations: Sincerity, or that forgiveness is owed.
lookFor: Acknowledgment of specific conduct and its impact
Offer of repair or a concrete change
'Sorry you feel that way' style non-apologies

concepts.title: Pursue and withdraw pattern
concepts.definition: One person presses for discussion or change while the other avoids or shuts down, and each move can intensify the other.
concepts.evidence: A meta-analysis linked this pattern to lower satisfaction and poorer outcomes for both people.
concepts.application: Names a cycle without blaming either side.
concepts.limitations: That withdrawing after a refusal, or to stay safe, is conflict avoidance.
lookFor: Repeated pressing for discussion met by avoidance or exit
Withdrawal that follows a refusal or a safety request (code separately)

concepts.title: Betrayal trauma and institutional betrayal
concepts.definition: Harm from someone (or an institution) a person depends on can be especially damaging and harder to see clearly.
concepts.evidence: Betrayal trauma theory proposes that dependence can promote 'blindness' to betrayal. Institutional betrayal, when an organisation fails to prevent or respond well to harm, is associated with worse outcomes.
concepts.application: Context for disclosures and for third-party or community involvement.
concepts.limitations: That a participant betrayed anyone.
lookFor: Disclosure of harm by someone the speaker depends on
Reports of an organisation's response to harm

concepts.title: DARVO: Deny, Attack, Reverse Victim and Offender
concepts.definition: A response to being held accountable that denies the behaviour, attacks the person raising it, and recasts the accused as the real victim.
concepts.evidence: Introduced by Freyd (1997). Experiments show DARVO makes observers find the accused more credible and the accuser less credible. A 2026 18-item short questionnaire found reported exposure to DARVO predicted trauma symptoms.
concepts.application: Subtext flags a possible DARVO sequence only when all three parts appear in response to a specific concern, and quotes each part.
concepts.limitations: That denial alone is DARVO; that DARVO-like wording proves the original concern is true; that a valid stop request is a role reversal.
lookFor: Denial of the specific conduct raised
Attack on the credibility or character of the person raising it
Claim that the accused is the real victim, in the same exchange

concepts.title: Gaslighting
concepts.definition: A pattern of undermining someone's confidence in their own perceptions, memory or sanity, usually within an unequal relationship.
concepts.evidence: Sociological work ties gaslighting to power and stereotypes of irrationality. A 2024 scale measures exposure to gaslighting and links it to psychological abuse and depression. Tolerance of gaslighting is linked to relationship power.
concepts.application: Flags repeated 'you're imagining it / you're crazy' moves over a pattern, quoted, and always considers honest memory differences.
concepts.limitations: That one disagreement or a different memory is gaslighting.
lookFor: Repeated statements that the other person is imagining, crazy or too sensitive
Denial of documented words that appear earlier in the same transcript

concepts.title: Different memories of the same event
concepts.definition: Honest people often remember the same event differently, and memory can change after the fact.
concepts.evidence: Decades of experiments show memory is reconstructive and can be altered by later information.
concepts.application: Keeps memory disputes neutral and separates 'what each person reports' from 'what happened'.
concepts.limitations: That any account is false or a 'false memory'.
lookFor: Conflicting accounts of an earlier event, each stated as a report

concepts.title: Why Subtext does not detect lies
concepts.definition: Neither people nor computers can reliably tell lies from truth by wording or style.
concepts.evidence: People average about 54% accuracy; linguistic cues to deception have small, context-dependent effects.
concepts.application: Subtext never labels a statement as a lie; it compares statements with each other and with the record.
concepts.limitations: Truthfulness of any statement from its language.
lookFor: Contradictions between statements within the record (report them; do not label lies)

concepts.title: Coercive control
concepts.definition: A pattern of behaviour over time that restricts someone's freedom through intimidation, isolation, monitoring, degradation or control of resources.
concepts.evidence: Recognised in law in England and Wales and elsewhere. Coercion can be defined as a demand backed by a credible threatened consequence. Survivors describe fear, unpredictability and loss of agency. Coding from text is more reliable with explicit behavioural examples. It occurs in all relationship forms, including immigration-related threats.
concepts.application: Subtext codes specific quoted behaviours (demand plus threatened consequence, isolation requests, monitoring) and states plainly whether one transcript can show a pattern.
concepts.limitations: That a single argument, a firm boundary or ordinary negotiation is coercive control.
lookFor: A demand plus a stated consequence
Requests to cut off friends or family
Monitoring of phone, location, money or movement
Rules with punishments

concepts.title: Technology-facilitated coercive control
concepts.definition: Using phones, apps, accounts or location sharing to monitor, threaten or control a partner.
concepts.evidence: Government guidance lists digital monitoring as controlling behaviour. Practice guidance warns that telling victim-survivors to stop using technology may not improve safety and can increase victim-blaming.
concepts.application: Supports a monitoring filter and safety-aware scripts.
concepts.limitations: That freely agreed location or password sharing is control.
lookFor: Demands for passwords, location or message access
Threats to share images or private messages

concepts.title: Consent
concepts.definition: Consent is each person's own, specific, ongoing agreement to a particular activity. It can be withdrawn.
concepts.evidence: Research separates inner willingness, explicit agreement and behaviour that others interpret as agreement, and shows how often people rely on ambiguous cues. Freezing under threat is common enough that absence of resistance cannot be read as consent.
concepts.application: Consent is never treated as a bargaining position. Another partner's wishes or a group agreement cannot stand in for one person's agreement. The same standard applies to everyone.
concepts.limitations: Whether consent was present in a reported event.
lookFor: A refusal, hesitation or stop request and what happens next
Another partner's or the group's wishes used as a reason for someone to agree

concepts.title: Going along with sex you don't want
concepts.definition: Agreeing to sex one does not desire. It differs from coercion, but pressure can turn compliance into coercion.
concepts.evidence: Compliance happens in many relationships. A 2025 Finnish study found partner sexual coercion and sexual distress were the strongest predictors of negative consequences, while approach motives predicted positive ones.
concepts.application: Gives users language between 'fine' and 'assault' without deciding for them.
concepts.limitations: Which category a specific encounter belongs to.
lookFor: Statements of going along with something unwanted
Pressure after a no

concepts.title: Consensual non-monogamy and relationship structure
concepts.definition: Open relationships, polyamory, throuples and other consensually non-monogamous structures.
concepts.evidence: A 2025 meta-analysis of 35 studies found no difference in relationship or sexual satisfaction between monogamous and CNM people. People still judge CNM relationships more harshly. Hierarchy between primary and secondary partners is common and measurable.
concepts.application: Structure is never a red flag. Subtext examines agreements, decision power and freedom to refuse inside whatever structure people chose, and distinguishes openly chosen hierarchy from imposed or undisclosed inequality.
concepts.limitations: That CNM, hierarchy, jealousy or different desires show mistreatment.
lookFor: Agreements within each pair versus the whole group
Who can veto, renegotiate or leave
Hierarchy described openly versus imposed

concepts.title: Foot-in-the-door, door-in-the-face, low-ball
concepts.definition: Request sequences that raise agreement: small then large, large then small, or agree then change the terms.
concepts.evidence: Classic studies found all three; door-in-the-face replicated in 2021, and a 2025 meta-analysis found its effect is real but small.
concepts.application: Names the sequence and the effect size, and checks whether terms changed after agreement.
concepts.limitations: That a sequence was a deliberate tactic.
lookFor: A small agreement followed by a bigger related ask
A large ask, refused, followed by a smaller one
Terms changed after someone agreed

concepts.title: Neuroscience of persuasion
concepts.definition: Studies of how the brain responds to persuasive messages.
concepts.evidence: Group-level responses in valuation and self-related regions can predict population behaviour change.
concepts.application: Educational card only.
concepts.limitations: That anyone was 'neurologically manipulated'.

concepts.title: Mirroring and tactical empathy
concepts.definition: Repeating or matching another person's words or manner to build rapport (popularised by Chris Voss).
concepts.evidence: Laboratory negotiators who subtly mimicked counterparts reached more agreements; evidence in intimate conflict is lacking.
concepts.application: Offered as an optional practitioner technique with a note that it can feel manipulative if noticed.
concepts.limitations: That mirroring obliges anyone to keep negotiating a boundary.
lookFor: Repeating the other person's last words as a question

concepts.title: Moral disengagement
concepts.definition: Ways people avoid feeling responsible for harm: justifying it, softening its name, comparing it to worse, shifting responsibility, minimising effects or blaming the person harmed.
concepts.evidence: Higher moral disengagement is associated with more harmful conduct; the framework is widely used and still debated.
concepts.application: Each mechanism is quoted and paired with a charitable alternative reading.
concepts.limitations: That a justification proves harm, or that a person is 'morally disengaged'.
lookFor: Justifying conduct by a higher purpose
Softened names for harm
'At least I didn't…' comparisons
Blaming the person affected

concepts.title: Cognitive dissonance
concepts.definition: Discomfort when actions conflict with beliefs, which people may reduce by changing their beliefs or justifications.
concepts.evidence: A brain study found activity during counter-attitudinal arguing predicted later attitude change.
concepts.application: Hypothesis label for possible rationalisation, never a finding.
concepts.limitations: That a participant is rationalising.
lookFor: Changing justifications for the same conduct over the conversation

concepts.title: Motivated reasoning and the bias blind spot
concepts.definition: Wanting a conclusion shapes how people weigh evidence, and people see bias more easily in others than in themselves.
concepts.evidence: Robust findings across decades of research.
concepts.application: Applies to all participants, to the user and to the analysis; supports the 'sanity check is not agreement' principle.
concepts.limitations: Which person in a dispute is biased.
lookFor: Evidence accepted from one side and dismissed from the other by the same standard

concepts.title: Intuition first, reasons second
concepts.definition: Moral judgments often come from quick intuitions, with reasons found afterwards. 'Two systems' is a useful metaphor, not two brain systems.
concepts.evidence: Haidt's social intuitionist model is influential and debated; critics argue the fast/slow divide is not clean.
concepts.application: Hypothesis label for 'possible post-hoc justification'.
concepts.limitations: That a participant's reasons are not genuine.
lookFor: Strong conclusions stated before reasons
Reasons that shift when challenged

concepts.title: Willpower 'running out' (ego depletion)
concepts.definition: The idea that self-control is a limited resource that gets used up.
concepts.evidence: A 23-lab preregistered replication found an effect near zero.
concepts.application: Subtext does not explain behaviour by depleted willpower or decision fatigue.
concepts.limitations: That tiredness or overload caused a participant's choices.

concepts.title: Triangulation (drawing in a third person)
concepts.definition: Pulling a third person into a two-person conflict, for example as ally, messenger or reason.
concepts.evidence: Bowen family-systems theory describes triangles; empirical work with families shows children drawn into parents' conflicts fare worse. Research on adult triads and polycules is limited.
concepts.application: Maps who is discussed, who is absent and whose wishes are used as reasons, and treats any alliance as tentative.
concepts.limitations: That mentioning or consulting a third person is coercive, or that a temporary alliance is a coordinated plan.
lookFor: An absent person's feelings used as the reason for a request
Messages carried through a third person
Two people aligning against a third

concepts.title: Gender and conversational style
concepts.definition: Popular books describe men and women as speaking different 'languages'.
concepts.evidence: Meta-analysis shows average gender differences in talkativeness and assertive or affiliative speech are small and depend on context.
concepts.application: Tannen's ideas can describe styles, never explain a person by gender.
concepts.limitations: Anything about a participant from their gender.

concepts.title: Trauma bond and Stockholm syndrome
concepts.definition: Popular terms for attachment to someone who causes harm.
concepts.evidence: 'Traumatic bonding' was studied in 1993 and linked to intermittent abuse and power imbalance. 'Stockholm syndrome' has no validated diagnostic criteria. 'Appeasement' has been proposed as a replacement.
concepts.application: Explains the terms and why leaving can be hard, in plain language.
concepts.limitations: That a relationship is a 'trauma bond' or a person has 'Stockholm syndrome'.

sources.citation: Poldrack, R. A. (2006). Can cognitive processes be inferred from neuroimaging data?. Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 10(2), 59–63. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tics.2005.12.004
sources.claim: 'Reverse inference' (concluding that a mental process occurred because a brain region was active) is weak evidence unless that region responds selectively to that process, which most regions do not.
sources.cannotEstablish: Group-level brain data cannot show what any participant in a transcript felt, intended, or experienced, and cannot be used to diagnose anyone.
sources.limitations: Methodological argument; it does not rule out all brain-based inference, it sets conditions for it.
